headline: Day one at the Lakeside Weekender: confetti, pipes and static
standfirst: Our volunteer blogger tries to explain the science behind the weekend's opening acts
brief: Dev is great with crowds and not so great with physics. Spot the sentences that need fixing before the blog goes live.

body.t: The weekend opened with the confetti cannon, which fires a paper capsule at 20 metres per second at 30° above the horizontal.
At the highest point of its flight the capsule's acceleration is zero, because for that instant it has stopped rising.

options: Once the capsule has left the cannon, gravity stops acting on it, so there is no acceleration at any point of the flight.
The acceleration is 9.8 m s⁻² downwards all the way, including at the top, because gravity still acts.
The acceleration is largest at the top, because the capsule is moving slowest there and so gravity has the most effect on it.
feedback: Gravity acts on the capsule for the whole flight. Only the cannon's push stops when the capsule leaves it.
Gravity gives the same acceleration at every point, whatever the speed. Being slowest at the top does not change that.
err.fix: At the highest point of its flight the capsule's vertical velocity is momentarily zero, but its acceleration is still 9.8 m s⁻² downwards, because gravity is still acting on it.
keys: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration.
Acceleration is 9.8 m s⁻² downwards throughout the flight, ignoring air resistance.

body.t: Ignoring air resistance, its horizontal velocity stays at about 17 metres per second for the whole flight.
body.ok: It is correct: the horizontal component is 20 cos 30° ≈ 17 m s⁻¹, and with no horizontal force it stays constant.

body.t: The festival's laptop plotted a graph of the capsule's vertical displacement against time, and the gradient of that graph at any instant gives the capsule's acceleration at that instant.

options: The gradient of a displacement–time graph is the velocity; acceleration is the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
The gradient of a displacement–time graph gives the total distance travelled so far, and the acceleration is the area under it.
The gradient of a displacement–time graph does give the acceleration, but only on the parts where the line is perfectly straight.
feedback: Distance is not a gradient. A gradient is a rate of change: change in displacement per unit time.
Straight or curved, the gradient of a displacement–time graph is the velocity. On a curve you find it from the tangent at that point.
err.fix: The festival's laptop plotted a graph of the capsule's vertical displacement against time, and the gradient of that graph at any instant gives the capsule's vertical velocity at that instant.
keys: Acceleration is the gradient of velocity–time.

body.t: Backstage, the sound crew tested a tuning pipe that is closed at one end and 0.34 metres long.
Its fundamental standing wave has a wavelength of 0.34 metres, the same as the length of the pipe.

options: The wavelength is half the pipe length, 0.17 m, because the wave must have an antinode at each end of the pipe.
The wavelength is twice the pipe length, 0.68 m, because any pipe holds exactly half a wavelength in its fundamental.
A node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end: a quarter of a wavelength fits, so 1.36 m.
feedback: An antinode at each end describes a pipe open at both ends. This pipe is closed at one end, which forces a node there.
Half a wavelength fits in a pipe open at both ends. Here one end is closed, which changes the pattern.
err.fix: Its fundamental standing wave has a wavelength of 1.36 metres, four times the length of the pipe, because the pipe holds a quarter of a wavelength.
keys: Closed end = node, open end = antinode.

body.t: The next note this pipe can sound is at three times the fundamental frequency, because a pipe closed at one end supports only odd harmonics.
body.ok: It is correct: with a node at one end and an antinode at the other, only odd numbers of quarter-wavelengths fit, giving frequencies f, 3f, 5f and so on.

body.t: Over in the craft tent, volunteers rubbed two balloons on a wool jumper so that each carried the same charge, and held them apart for visitors.
Dev explained that if you double the distance between the balloons, the repulsive force between them halves.

options: The force stays the same, because it depends only on the size of the two charges and not on how far apart they are.
The force becomes four times smaller, because Coulomb's law is an inverse square law.
The force doubles, because the balloons have more room in which to push against each other, so the repulsion builds up.
feedback: The force depends on the distance as well as on the charges: $F \propto q_1 q_2 / r^2$.
Moving charges further apart weakens the force between them. It does not strengthen it.
err.fix: Dev explained that if you double the distance between the balloons, the repulsive force between them becomes a quarter of its original value.

body.t: A balloon that has gained electrons can still stick to a neutral wall, because the wall's charges are slightly separated, with the nearer ones opposite in sign to the balloon's.
body.ok: It is correct: the wall becomes polarised, with its nearer charges opposite in sign to the balloon's. The attraction to the nearer charges is slightly stronger than the repulsion from the farther ones.

body.t: The electric field lines around one of these balloons point away from it, because it has gained electrons.

options: Field lines always point away from any charged object, whatever its sign, because they show where the field spreads out to.
Field lines show the path the electrons take as they leave the balloon, so they point away from it.
Field lines show the force on a positive test charge, so around a negative balloon they point towards it.
feedback: The direction depends on the sign of the charge. Lines point away from positive charges and towards negative ones.
Field lines show the force on a positive test charge. They are not the paths of electrons, which in any case stay on the balloon.
err.fix: The electric field lines around one of these balloons point towards it, because it has gained electrons and so is negatively charged.
keys: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive test charge.
A negatively charged object has lines pointing towards it.
